540.title: Gamaliel's advice (Acts 5:34–39)
540.hook: if it's of men it will fail, if of God you can't stop it
540.howItsDone: The Church often waits years before approving a new religious community or a claimed private revelation, testing it over time by its fruits and its fidelity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekklēsia, the assembly shaken by a hard story Luke kept. Your line was the bible keeps the hard stories. What did you stop polishing? Day five hundred forty.

Voices are rising in a meeting. Someone is ready to fire someone. Then an older colleague raises a hand and says, wait. Let's not decide this today. Give it six months and see. The apostles have been arrested again, and again they've kept preaching. Back before the council, Peter says, we ought to obey God, rather than men. The council is furious. Luke says some of them want to kill the apostles. And then a man stands up and asks for the room.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SAYS, WAIT.` → `ARRESTED AGAIN.` → `A MAN ASKS FOR THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Luke introduces him with respect: a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people. Later in Acts, Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. And the Mishnah, the great early collection of Jewish teaching, says that when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased. He has the apostles taken outside, and then he speaks to his colleagues. He reminds them of men who came before: a Theudas who gathered about four hundred followers, a Judas of Galilee who stirred up people in the days of the census. Both were killed, and their movements scattered and came to nothing. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "for if this council or this work be of men, it will come to nought; But if it be of God, you cannot overthrow it, lest perhaps you be found even to fight against God." The council listens. Instead of a death sentence, the apostles are beaten, ordered again not to speak in Jesus's name, and released. And Luke says they leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for the name. Gamaliel isn't a follower of Jesus here. He's a careful, devout teacher of his own tradition giving honest advice: don't force it, let God and time show what this is. Christians have often reached for his test when something new appears in the Church: a movement, an order, an idea. Some religious communities that began under suspicion, or were even disbanded for a time, were later recognized because they lasted and bore fruit.
screen: `A PHARISEE, HONORED BY ALL.` · `THEUDAS AND JUDAS: CAME TO NOTHING.` · `IF IT BE OF GOD.` · `LET TIME SHOW WHAT IT IS.` · then, large: `GAMALIEL'S ADVICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let time test something. Sit and breathe. Think of something you're in a hurry to judge: a new person at work, a change at church or in your family, an idea you don't trust, a plan someone else is excited about. Notice the urge to settle it now. Then picture setting it on a shelf with a date on it, three months away. Breathe out the hurry. If you pray, you can hold Gamaliel's words, if it be of God, and leave the outcome there. If you don't, just let it wait. The bell holds the time.
Gamaliel's advice. A respected Pharisee tells the council to leave the apostles alone: if this is of God, you can't stop it. Today's word.
Your line: if it be of god. Today, when you want to shut something down quickly, say let's see, and give it time. Day five hundred forty.

he urged the council to leave them alone and let God show.
Paul later says he studied under Gamaliel
Acts 22:3: brought up at the feet of Gamaliel.
the apostles left the council discouraged
they left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for the name.

fork.setup: you're on the council. the apostles keep preaching after you've forbidden it, and some want them dead. what does Gamaliel advise?
options: make an example of them.
leave them alone; if it's of God you can't stop it.
exile them from Jerusalem.
fork.reveal: if it be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, you cannot overthrow it, lest you be found to fight against God.

original.note: Greek: fighters against God (Acts 5:39), the danger Gamaliel warns of.

trapdoor: what you thought: an enemy of the Church who happened to help.
what it means: a devout and respected teacher of the law giving honest advice: let God and time show what this is.
what a scholar hears: the Mishnah (Sotah 9:15) honors Rabban Gamaliel the Elder; Josephus dates a Theudas later than this speech, a long-discussed puzzle.

541.title: The seven (Acts 6:1–7)
541.hook: widows are neglected, and seven are chosen to serve tables
541.howItsDone: In the Catholic Church deacons are ordained by a bishop; at Mass they proclaim the Gospel, and they may baptize, witness marriages and lead funerals, with a special charge to serve the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gamaliel's advice to the council: let time show. Your line was if it be of god. What did you give time to? Day five hundred forty-one.

Every growing group hits the same wall. A church, a school, a startup, a family business: at first everyone knows everyone, and things just get done. Then it doubles. Someone gets forgotten, a complaint starts in the hallway, and it turns out the people on one side of the room have been overlooked. The early Church in Jerusalem hit that wall fast. A fast-growing community, a daily distribution of food for widows, and two groups who spoke different languages. Someone was being left out.
screen: `EVERY GROWING GROUP HITS A WALL.` → `A DAILY DISTRIBUTION.` → `SOMEONE LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: Luke names the two groups. The Hellenists, Jewish believers who spoke Greek, many probably from abroad, and the Hebrews, who spoke Aramaic and were from the land. The Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the daily ministration, the daily serving of food. That's a real complaint, and Luke doesn't hide it. The twelve call everyone together and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables." That's not snobbery about waiting tables. It's honesty about limits. They can't do everything well. So they ask the community to pick seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of it, and the apostles will keep to prayer and the ministry of the word. Here's a detail worth noticing: all seven have Greek names. Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert from Antioch. The group that was overlooked gets leaders who know it from the inside. The apostles pray and lay their hands on them. And Luke says the word of God grew, and the number of disciples multiplied greatly. The word deacon comes from the Greek diakonos, a servant, and Luke's word for that daily serving, diakonia, is the same family. Acts never actually calls the seven deacons, but Catholic tradition has long seen them as the first. Today a deacon is ordained; he proclaims the Gospel at Mass, baptizes, witnesses marriages, leads funerals, and is meant above all to serve the poor. Stephen, the first named, would soon be killed for his witness; tradition calls him the first martyr. And tomorrow, we follow another of the seven: Philip.
screen: `TWO LANGUAGES, ONE TABLE.` · `WE CAN'T DO EVERYTHING WELL.` · `SEVEN GREEK NAMES.` · `DIAKONIA: THE DAILY SERVING.` · then, large: `DEACON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people who serve. Sit and breathe. If you know a deacon, bring him to mind. If not, think of whoever quietly serves the tables where you are: the volunteer at the food pantry, the person who sets up chairs, the nurse on the night shift, the parent packing lunches. Picture their hands at work. Then think of anyone around you who might be overlooked, the way those widows were. If you pray, you can pray for a deacon, or for them. If you don't, just hold them with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Deacon. From the Greek diakonos, a servant: the ministry the Church traces to the seven chosen to serve tables in Acts. Today's word.
Your line: serve the tables. Today, notice who's being left out of something, a conversation, a meal, a group chat, and bring them in. Day five hundred forty-one.

pairs: not leave the word of God to serve tables

fork.setup: you're one of the twelve. the Greek-speaking widows are being missed in the daily food, and you can't do it all. what do you do?
options: take over the food yourselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: deacons are assistant priests.
what it means: the ministry of service, traced to seven chosen so no one would be overlooked at the table.
what a scholar hears: Acts 6 uses diakonia (6:1, 4) and diakonein (6:2), not diakonos; Irenaeus already links Stephen to the diaconate; Vatican II restored the permanent diaconate (Lumen Gentium 29).

542.title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
542.hook: how can I understand unless someone shows me
542.howItsDone: Catholics are taught the faith through catechesis: in parishes, adults preparing for baptism walk with a sponsor and catechists through the scriptures before receiving the sacraments, often at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven chosen so the widows wouldn't be forgotten, the first deacons. Your line was serve the tables. Whose table did you serve? Day five hundred forty-two.

A desert road, south out of Jerusalem toward Gaza, in the heat of the day. A chariot is rolling home. In it sits a powerful man, the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, a court official the text calls a eunuch. He has traveled a very long way to worship in Jerusalem, and now he's going home with a scroll in his lap, reading aloud, the way people often read then. And he's stuck. He can make out every word and still can't tell what it means. Anyone who has read a contract, a diagnosis, or a hard page of scripture knows exactly how that feels.
screen: `A DESERT ROAD TO GAZA.` → `A TREASURER WITH A SCROLL.` → `EVERY WORD, AND NO MEANING.`

segments.voice: An angel sends Philip, one of the seven from yesterday, to that empty road. The Spirit tells him: go near, join that chariot. So Philip runs alongside, hears the man reading the prophet Isaiah, and asks a plain question: do you understand what you're reading? The answer, in the Douay-Rheims, is disarmingly plain: "And how can I, unless some man shew me?" Then he invites Philip up to sit with him. Notice who is asking. Not a beginner with no learning, but a court official who can read, who owns a scroll, who traveled a very long way to pray. He isn't embarrassed to say, I need someone. And Philip doesn't lecture from the road. He climbs in and sits beside him. The passage is Isaiah's servant, led like a sheep to the slaughter and silent before his shearer. The man asks: is the prophet talking about himself, or someone else? Beginning from that very scripture, Philip tells him about Jesus. Then they pass water, and the man says, "See, here is water: what doth hinder me from being baptized?" Nothing does. The chariot stops, both go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him. Then Philip is gone, and the man "went on his way rejoicing." Where was he from? The Greek says Ethiopia, which then meant the kingdom of Kush, up the Nile, south of Egypt. Ethiopian Christians today love this man as one of their own first believers. Catholics see the whole Church's way of teaching here: scripture, a guide who sits beside you, and then the sacrament.
screen: `DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU READ?` · `HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOME MAN SHOW ME?` · `PHILIP CLIMBS IN AND SITS DOWN.` · `HERE IS WATER.` · then, large: `HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one thing kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has asked you something lately, a coworker stuck on a task, a kid with homework, a parent with a new phone. Remember how they asked. Now picture doing what Philip did: not answering from the road, but climbing in and sitting beside them. Slow. No sighing. Starting from where they are. And notice, too, the thing you don't understand yet, and who you might ask. If you pray, you can ask for the patience of someone who runs alongside a chariot. The bell holds the time.
Ethiopian. The court official from the kingdom of Kush, honest enough to say he needed help understanding scripture, baptized by Philip on a desert road. Today's word.
Your line: how can I, unless. Today, ask one honest question about something you don't understand, or answer one kindly. Day five hundred forty-two.

what doth hinder me from being baptized?

he was the queen's treasurer, reading Isaiah aloud from his own scroll. he just needed a guide.
Philip was one of the seven chosen to serve tables
the same Philip from the day before: a deacon, now sent to a desert road.
in the text, Ethiopia means the same country as on today's maps
it meant Kush, the kingdom up the Nile south of Egypt.

fork.setup: you're Philip. a stranger in a chariot is reading Isaiah aloud on a desert road. what do you do?
options: wait for him to stop and ask you.
run up and ask if he understands it.

fork.reveal: he runs alongside and asks a question. the man invites him up, and Philip sits beside him and starts from the very page he was reading.

original.note: Greek: Ethiopian. the word the text uses for the man from Kush, far up the Nile.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary meets a foreigner and converts him.
what it means: a powerful, learned man admits he needs a guide, and a deacon climbs in and sits beside him before he says a word about Jesus.

what a scholar hears: Ethiopia in the Greek meant Kush, on the upper Nile, and Candace was a royal title there, not a personal name. Luke places a man from the far south of the known world among the first baptized.

543.title: Ananias of Damascus (Acts 9:10–19)
543.hook: he's afraid of Saul, goes anyway, and calls him brother
543.howItsDone: Catholics honor Ananias of Damascus as a saint, and they hear this passage at Mass in the Easter season and on the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip and the Ethiopian: a chariot, a scroll, and an honest question. Your line was how can I, unless. Did you ask, or explain, something kindly? Day five hundred forty-three.

Saul on the road to Damascus, the light, the fall, the voice: that's the half of this story painters love. The second half belongs to a man who appears for only a few verses. His name is Ananias. He's a disciple living in Damascus. He isn't an apostle, he leaves no letters, and he has heard all about Saul: the man who has been dragging believers off to prison. And one day the Lord tells Ananias to go and find him.
screen: `THE FAMOUS HALF: THE ROAD.` → `THE OTHER HALF: ANANIAS.` → `GO AND FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: The instructions are oddly precise. In the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, and go into the street that is called Strait," and seek, in the house of Judas, one named Saul of Tarsus. He's praying, and he's blind. And Ananias does something very human. He argues. Lord, I've heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem, and he's here with authority to arrest everyone who calls on your name. That's not a lack of faith. It's simple memory. He knows exactly who Saul is. The answer doesn't take the danger away. Go thy way, the Lord says, "for this man is to me a vessel of election," to carry my name before the Gentiles. So Ananias goes. Picture the walk down that street, the knock, the blind man who once came to arrest people like him. And the first two words out of Ananias's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims, are these: "Brother Saul." Not enemy. Not persecutor. Brother. He lays his hands on him, and immediately something like scales falls from Saul's eyes. He sees, he gets up, he is baptized, and he eats. The future apostle Paul is welcomed into the Church by a disciple who appears for only a few verses. Tradition places the street called Straight on the long main street of old Damascus. And Ananias is honored as a saint: a frightened man who knocked anyway.
screen: `THE STREET CALLED STRAIGHT.` · `ANANIAS ARGUES: I KNOW THIS MAN.` · `A VESSEL OF ELECTION.` · `SCALES FALL FROM HIS EYES.` · then, large: `BROTHER SAUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to someone you fear. Not physically dangerous, just hard. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you avoid: the one who hurt you, the one who intimidates you, the conversation you keep postponing. Notice what your body does when you picture them. Ananias felt that too, and said so out loud. Now imagine your first two words if you went. What would it sound like to start with something like brother, or sister, or friend? You don't have to go today. Just let the picture sit. If you pray, you can tell God plainly what you're afraid of, the way Ananias did. The bell holds the time.
Brother. The first word Ananias said to Saul, the man he feared, instead of enemy or persecutor. Today's word.
Your line: brother saul. Today, when you meet someone you'd rather avoid, let your first word be a kind one. Day five hundred forty-three.

blind, praying, at the house of Judas

options: refuse; it's a trap.

original.note: Greek: brother. the first word Ananias says to the man he feared.

trapdoor: what you thought: the conversion of Paul was a light on the road, and that was all.
what it means: blind and praying, Saul needs a frightened stranger to come, lay hands on him, and call him brother before he sees again.

what a scholar hears: the story is told three times in Acts: by Luke in chapter 9, and by Paul in chapters 22 and 26. Ananias appears in the first two. tradition identifies the street called Straight with the long straight street of old Damascus.

544.title: Tabitha, arise (Acts 9:36–42)
544.hook: the widows show Peter the coats she made them
544.carry: she was full of good works
544.howItsDone: Many Catholic parishes keep groups that sew, knit or cook for the poor, the sick and new mothers, and Tabitha is honored as a saint, traditionally on October 25.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananias, afraid, walking down the street called Straight. Your line was brother Saul. Was your first word a kind one? Day five hundred forty-four.

An upstairs room in Joppa, a port town on the coast. A woman has died, and her body has been washed and laid out. The room is full of widows, and they are crying. When Peter arrives, they don't make speeches about her. They do something better. They hold up their clothes. Coats, tunics, garments, all made by her hands. This one she sewed for me. This one too. It's a eulogy made of fabric. A sweater someone knitted, a quilt a grandmother made: some things keep a person close.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN JOPPA.` → `THE WIDOWS ARE WEEPING.` → `A EULOGY MADE OF FABRIC.`

segments.voice: Her name was Tabitha. Luke translates it for his Greek readers: Dorcas. Both names mean gazelle. And Luke calls her, plainly, a disciple, using the feminine form of the word. The Douay-Rheims sums up her life in one line: "This woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did." Not full of opinions, or plans. Full of works. When she falls sick and dies, the disciples hear that Peter is in Lydda, close by, and send two men: please come without delay. He comes. The widows show him the coats and garments she made while she was with them. And Peter does something that echoes a scene he once watched. He sends everyone out of the room, kneels, and prays. Then he turns to the body and says, "Tabitha, arise." She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up. He gives her his hand, lifts her, and calls the saints and the widows to see her alive. Years before, Peter stood in a room where Jesus took a dead girl by the hand and said, in Aramaic, talitha cumi: little girl, arise. Talitha and Tabitha are one letter apart. Whether Luke meant the echo or not, Peter is doing what he saw his teacher do. And notice why the town cared so much: not because she was powerful, but because she clothed people nobody else clothed. Later, church sewing circles that made clothes for the poor were often called Dorcas societies, after her.
screen: `TABITHA, DORCAS: GAZELLE.` · `FULL OF GOOD WORKS.` · `THE COATS SHE MADE THEM.` · `PETER KNEELS AND PRAYS.` · then, large: `TABITHA, ARISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make something for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of what your hands can make. Not everyone sews. Maybe you cook, or fix bikes, or write, or draw, or fold a really good paper crane. Now think of one person who could use something made by you, and not bought. A note in your own handwriting counts. A meal counts. Picture handing it to them. Notice how small and real it is. If you pray, you can offer your hands for the day. The bell holds the time.
Tabitha. Dorcas, the gazelle of Joppa, a disciple whose good works were coats on widows' backs, raised when Peter said arise. Today's word.
Your line: she was full of good works. Today, make one thing with your own hands and give it away. Day five hundred forty-four.

what it means: a town grieves a woman because she clothed the widows nobody clothed, and Peter does what he saw Jesus do.

545.title: Christians (Acts 11:19–26)
545.hook: in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians
545.howItsDone: Catholics receive their Christian name at baptism, often a saint's name, and the Church keeps the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, which once had a separate celebration for Peter's chair at Antioch.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tabitha of Joppa, and the coats she made for the widows. Your line was she was full of good works. What did your hands make? Day five hundred forty-five.

For the first years after Jesus, his followers didn't have one name. In Acts they're the disciples, the brethren, the saints, the believers, and people of the Way. Nobody had a word on a sign outside a building. Then, in a big, noisy, mixed city in Syria, somebody gave them a name. The text doesn't say who. And the name stuck. It started in a single city, at a single moment, and Luke wrote the moment down.
screen: `DISCIPLES, BRETHREN, THE WAY.` → `NO ONE NAME YET.` → `THEN, ONE CITY.`

segments.voice: The city is Antioch, a great city of Roman Syria. After Stephen's death, believers scattered, and spoke the word only to fellow Jews. But some men from Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch and spoke to Greeks as well, and a great number believed. Jerusalem hears and sends Barnabas, the son of encouragement. He sees what's happening, and the text says he was glad. Then he does something wise: he goes to Tarsus to find Saul, the new convert from Damascus, and brings him back. The two of them teach in Antioch for a whole year. And then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "at Antioch the disciples were first named Christians." In Greek, Christianoi. The ending is a Latin-style one, used for a party or a household: Caesar's people, Herod's people. So the name likely meant Christ's people, the Messiah's crowd. Some readers think outsiders coined it, maybe half as a joke. The word turns up again from King Agrippa's lips later in Acts, and in First Peter, where believers are told not to be ashamed if they suffer as one. So a name perhaps given by neighbors became a name people were willing to die for. Antioch has another place in Catholic memory. Tradition says Peter led the church there before Rome. And a later bishop of Antioch, Ignatius, wrote a letter that calls the Church catholic, meaning universal.
screen: `ANTIOCH: JEWS AND GREEKS TOGETHER.` · `BARNABAS FETCHES SAUL.` · `CHRISTIANOI: CHRIST'S PEOPLE.` · `A NICKNAME BECOMES A NAME.` · then, large: `FIRST CALLED CHRISTIANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what the name asks. Settle, and breathe. Whatever name you carry, by faith or family or job, sit with it for a moment. If you are a Christian, notice that the word may first have come from neighbors who watched how believers lived. What would your neighbors call you, judging only by this past week? If the name isn't yours, think of a name you do carry, a family name, a team, a title, and what it asks of you. No grading. Just notice. If you pray, you can ask to live up to your name. The bell holds the time.
Christian. Christ's people, the Messiah's people, a name first heard in Antioch and perhaps given by outsiders. Today's word.
Your line: first called christians. Today, do one thing that would make sense of your name to someone watching. Day five hundred forty-five.

options: run it all yourself.
go to Tarsus and bring back Saul.
send to Jerusalem for the twelve.

original.note: Greek: Christian, one of Christ's people. Christos means anointed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the name Christians gave themselves.
what it means: in Antioch, where Jews and Greeks believed together, the disciples were first called by a name probably given by others.

what a scholar hears: the -ianos ending is a Latin-style party label, like Herodians. the word turns up again in Acts 26 and 1 Peter 4, and Ignatius of Antioch's letter to the Smyrnaeans is often cited as an early use of 'catholic church'.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Smyrnaeans 8

546.title: Rhoda at the gate (Acts 12:1–17)
546.hook: Peter escapes prison, and the maid is so glad she forgets to open the door
546.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saints Peter and Paul on June 29, and this reading of Peter's release from prison is the first reading at that day's Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. Your line was first called christians. What did your name ask of you? Day five hundred forty-six.

It's the middle of the night in Jerusalem, and a house is full of people praying. They have reason to. King Herod has just killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. And now Herod has arrested Peter, and plans to bring him out after the feast. So the church prays for him, hard, all night. Then someone knocks at the outer gate. And what happens next comes close to comedy.
screen: `JAMES IS KILLED.` → `PETER IS IN PRISON.` → `A HOUSE PRAYING ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the prison. Peter is asleep between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with guards at the door. An angel appears, light fills the cell, and the angel strikes Peter on the side: get up, quickly. The chains fall off. Put on your shoes, wrap your cloak, follow me. Peter thinks he's dreaming. They pass the first guard and the second, and the iron gate to the city opens by itself. Then the angel is gone, and Peter, standing alone in the street, realizes it's real. He goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where the church is praying. He knocks. A servant girl named Rhoda comes to answer. And in the Douay-Rheims: "as soon as she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for joy." She's so happy she runs inside to tell everyone and leaves him standing in the street. And the people praying for his release? They tell her she's out of her mind. She insists. Then they say it must be his angel. Meanwhile, the text says, "Peter continued knocking." Finally they open, and they are astonished. Peter waves them quiet, tells them how the Lord brought him out, and says: tell these things to James, and to the brethren. Then he leaves for another place. Luke doesn't hide how slow the praying church was to believe its own prayer had been answered. And the person who believed first was the servant at the door.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at an answered prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think back over a year or two. Was there something you hoped for, or prayed for, that actually came, and you barely noticed? A job, a phone call, a test result, a reconciliation. Maybe you were slow to believe it, like the room that told Rhoda she was mad. Let yourself smile at that. Rhoda's mistake was joy. Theirs was doubt. Either way, Peter got in. If you pray, you can say thank you for one thing you forgot to thank God for. The bell holds the time.
Rhoda. The servant girl so glad to hear Peter's voice that she forgot to let him in, and believed before anyone else did. Today's word.
